h1: Negotiating a rent free fit out period on a brewpub lease
title: Rent Free Fit Out on a Brewpub Lease | Craft Beer School
desc: How to negotiate a rent free fit out period on a brewpub lease: why a brewpub needs one, how to tie it to licences and what to ask the landlord.
teaser: A brewpub pays rent for months before it sells a single pint. The lease is where you fix that.
standfirst: A brewhouse, a kitchen and a licence take longer to open than an ordinary restaurant. If rent starts on the day you get the keys, you pay for months of an empty room. Here is how to ask for a fit out period and what to write into the lease.
sections: Why a brewpub needs more fit out time than a restaurant

A restaurant can often open within weeks of handover. A brewpub rarely can. The brewhouse and fermenters sit on a floor that has to carry their weight when full. The floor needs drains and slope. The cellar needs cooling, the kitchen needs an exhaust and the whole site needs enough power. Our guide on planning the electrical load for a brewpub shows how much of that work happens before a single tank arrives.

Then there is the licence. In India alcohol is a state subject, so the process, the inspections and the timeline differ from state to state and change through notifications. Ask a licensing consultant for the current sequence in your state. What matters for the lease is that you often cannot sell beer until the licence is issued. You often cannot complete the licence until the premises are built.

That is the argument you take to the landlord. The rent clock should not start before you can trade.
What a landlord is really worried about

A landlord hears "rent free" and thinks of a tenant who might walk away. Your job is to answer that worry before it is raised.

Show the landlord the money you are putting into the building: tiles, drains, electrics, plumbing and kitchen ducting that stay behind if you leave. Fit out spend improves the property. Explain that the fit out period is a fixed number of months with a plan behind it, not an open ended favour.

Offer something in return. A longer lock-in, a larger security deposit or a rent that steps up after opening all show commitment. Landlords generally prefer a firm lock-in to a small rent discount.
Three ways to structure the rent free period

There are three common structures. Choose the one that fits your project risk.

  • Fixed months. Rent starts a set number of months after handover. It is simple, but if the licence runs late you pay rent while still closed.
  • Tied to a trigger. Rent starts on the earlier of the licence date plus a short grace period or an outside date. This protects you from licence delay and protects the landlord from endless waiting.
  • Stepped rent. A low rent during fit out, a reduced rent for the first months of trading, then the full rate. This suits landlords who want some income from day one.

Whatever you choose, write the outside date down. A trigger with no outside date is the clause landlords reject.
Work out what the free months are worth

Put numbers on it before you negotiate. Here is an illustration with round, made up figures. A site at ₹3 lakh a month with a four month fit out period is worth ₹12 lakh of rent you do not pay before opening. If the licence adds two months of delay and the clause only covers four, you pay ₹6 lakh of rent on a closed pub.

Now compare with trading. Our guide on rent as a share of revenue shows how to test what rent the pub can carry once it is open. A generous rent free period on a rent that is too high is not a good deal. Check both together.

Use your own quotes for the fit out timeline, not a guess. Ask your contractor for a week by week programme and give the landlord the same dates.
Clauses that matter as much as the free months

The rent free period is one line in a long document. Read the rest for these:

  • Permission to carry out structural work, drilling, drain cutting and rooftop or wall exhaust, with a clear process for approvals.
  • Who owns the fixtures and what you must remove or restore when the lease ends.
  • Rights to a dedicated water tank, utility connections and a separate power meter or load increase.
  • Signage rights, including a brewery name on the front.
  • A clause that lets you end the lease or pause rent if the licence is refused for reasons outside your control.

Brewery equipment is heavy and the layout is fixed once drains are cut. Check the plan in brewpub layout against what the landlord permits before you sign.

This is a guide to the questions, not legal advice. A lease is a binding contract and the stamp duty, registration and tenancy rules differ by state. Have a property lawyer read it. Ask them specifically about the rent commencement clause, the lock-in and what happens if the licence is delayed or refused.

Keep every promise in the document. A verbal assurance about "we will sort the rent when you open" is worth nothing when the landlord changes or sells the building.
The skill behind a good lease

A founder who walks into the landlord meeting with a fit out programme, a licence timeline and a rent test has a much better chance than one who asks for a discount. That preparation is the same work as a brewpub business plan: cash flow by month, costs before revenue and the point at which the pub breaks even. We cover that in Brewery Business Management, because lease terms are far easier to defend when the model behind them is sound.
faqs: How long a rent free period should a brewpub ask for?

It depends on your fit out programme and your state's licence timeline. Build the dates from your contractor's schedule and a licensing adviser's estimate, then ask for rent to start on a licence trigger with an outside date.
Will a landlord agree to rent free months?
Often yes, if you show the money you are spending on the building and offer a lock-in or a deposit in return. A fixed, planned period is easier to agree than an open ended one.
Should rent start when I get the keys?
Not for a brewpub. The site cannot trade until the build is finished and the licence is issued, so the clause should link rent to one of those events.
Do I need a lawyer for the lease?
Yes. Stamp duty, registration and tenancy rules differ between states. A property lawyer should read the rent commencement and lock-in clauses before you sign.
